name-us-state-as-big-as-england: Mid-sized states of the east and south: Alabama, Louisiana, New York, North Carolina.
name-us-state-as-big-as-uk: The big square states of the west: Oregon, Wyoming, Colorado, Utah; Michigan with its lakes.
name-us-state-as-big-as-germany: Only the biggest states come close: Montana, New Mexico, California, Arizona.
name-country-10-per-km2: Fermi: Russia has about 146 million people on 17 million square kilometres.
name-country-30-per-km2: Fermi: the US has about 340 million people on over 9 million square kilometres.
name-country-100-per-km2: Fermi: France has about 68 million people on about 550,000 square kilometres.
name-country-300-per-km2: Fermi: the UK has about 69 million people on 244,000 square kilometres.
milk-teeth: Start from yourself: an adult has 32, and a small child's jaw has room for fewer, with no wisdom teeth.
hand-bones: Check it yourself: three in each finger, two in the thumb, one more for each in the palm, and a cluster at the wrist.
london-population: Fermi from two anchors: the UK has about 69 million people, and about one in eight lives in its capital.
stonehenge-stones-height: Reason from yourself: in photos of visitors beside them, the stones are about twice a person's height.
glastonbury-capacity: Wembley holds 90,000; Glastonbury is a temporary city of tents a few times that.
bangkok-visitors: Thailand is one of the world's top tourist countries, and most of its visitors pass through Bangkok.
norway-winter-medals: Fermi: 24 Winter Games so far, and Norway, a winter-sport giant, often wins 20 to 40 at each.
italy-world-heritage-sites: Rome, Venice, Florence, Pompeii, Pisa, the Dolomites: count the famous places and the many old towns besides.
sahara-width: On a map it spans almost the whole width of northern Africa, about as wide as the United States.
giraffe-neck-bones: Reason from yourself: your own neck has a few small bones; a long neck might be longer bones, not more of them.
iceland-vegetation: Picture lava fields, glaciers and black sand, with green only in the lowlands and valleys.
switzerland-share-of-alps: On a map the Alps arc from France through Switzerland and Italy to Austria and Slovenia: Switzerland is one piece of five.
brain-share-of-weight: Fermi from two anchors: a brain weighs about as much as a bag of sugar, out of the 70 kg or so of you.
premier-league-matches: Check it yourself: 20 clubs, and each plays every other club at home and away.
ribs: Run a finger down your side: the ribs come in pairs, about a dozen on each side.
taste-bud-lifespan: A burnt tongue tastes normally again within a week or two, so taste buds must renew in days, not months.
yawn-length: Yawn now (reading this may help) and count: a slow breath in, a stretch, a quick breath out.
camel-drink: You might drink a litre when parched; a camel weighs as much as several people and refills its whole store at once.
blue-whale-calf-growth: A human baby puts on about 30 g a day at 3.5 kg; a blue whale calf is born weighing tonnes, hundreds of times more.
kangaroo-pregnancy: Kangaroos are marsupials: the baby is born tiny and does its growing in the pouch, so the pregnancy takes weeks, not months.
electric-eel-shock: Mains electricity is 230 V in Europe and 120 V in the US, and an eel's shock stuns a fish from a distance: a few times mains.
emperor-penguin-fast: The father waits out the Antarctic winter on the ice, far from the sea, for the whole incubation and more: months, not weeks.
lion-roar-distance: Thunder carries for kilometres, and a lion's roar rattles your chest at the zoo: a few kilometres to ten.
bear-species: Count the ones you know: polar, brown or grizzly, black, panda, then a few you half remember (sun, sloth, spectacled).
cat-claws: Picture a paw: four toes plus a dewclaw at the front; four paws, so about 16 to 20.
wild-sloth-sleep: Sloths are famous for doing nothing, so guess well above your own 8 hours; wild ones turn out busier than zoo ones.
koala-sleep: Koalas are famously sleepy, dozing in a tree all day: most of the day, well above 12 hours.
swift-time-aloft: Swifts arrive in summer, leave for Africa in autumn and are hardly ever seen perched: months on end in the air.
dairy-cow-milk: Picture a cow beside a few big milk bottles; it is milked twice a day and is far bigger than a goat: tens of litres.
mcdonalds-customers-a-day: Tens of thousands of restaurants, each serving a couple of thousand people a day: tens of millions.
french-baguettes-a-day: France has about 68 million people; if every other person buys one a day, that's over 30 million.
james-bond-films: Six actors have played Bond since the 1960s, most for three to seven films: about two dozen.
green-eggs-and-ham-words: Say it in your head: Sam, I, am, green, eggs, ham, like, not, house, mouse, box, fox... a tiny vocabulary, well under a hundred.
eras-tour-crowd: 149 stadium shows of 50,000 to 90,000 people each: multiply to about 10 million.
lord-of-the-rings-films-length: Each film is about three hours, famously long; three of them make about nine hours.
sistine-ceiling-time: One man painting a whole chapel ceiling in fresco, scene by scene: years, not months, but not a lifetime.
mozart-first-pieces: He's the classic child prodigy, performing for royalty as a small child, so composing very young indeed.
haiku-syllables: Remember the school rule: three lines of five, seven and five.
canada-flag-leaf-points: Picture the leaf: a top point, a few on each side of three lobes, and two at the base by the stem.
eu-flag-stars: Picture the circle of gold stars on blue: about a dozen, though you might expect one for each member.
jenga-blocks: Picture the starting tower: three blocks a layer, a bit under 20 layers tall.
greek-alphabet-letters: Count the ones you know from maths: alpha, beta, gamma, delta, pi, sigma, omega... a little under English's 26.
eu-official-languages: 27 countries, but some share a language (German, French, Dutch, Greek): a few fewer than 27.
concert-harp-strings: Picture an orchestra harp: taller than the player, strings packed close across its whole height: dozens, perhaps 40 to 50.
connect-four-holes: Picture the frame: seven columns, six rows.
tolkien-writing-time: A huge book written by a professor in his spare time, through the war years: about a decade.
shuttlecock-feathers: Picture the skirt: a ring of overlapping feathers around a cork, more than ten, fewer than twenty.
ten-thousand-metres-laps: A running track lap is 400 m, so 10 km is ten thousand over four hundred.
oldest-olympic-medallist: Shooting and riding reward experience over youth, so a medal at 60-plus sounds possible.
phelps-olympic-medals: He won 8 golds at one Games and swam at four or five Olympics: well over 20 in all.
messi-barcelona-goals: About 17 seasons, scoring 30 to 50 a season at his peak: several hundred.
super-bowl-2025-viewers: The US has about 340 million people and the Super Bowl is its biggest TV night: about a third of everyone.
ironman-distance: It ends with a whole marathon (42 km) after a bike ride several times as long and a swim of a few km.
bowling-perfect-score: Ten frames, and a strike scores 10 plus the next two balls: 30 a frame at most.
snooker-maximum-break: Fifteen reds at 1 point, each followed by the black at 7, then the six colours: about 150.
pele-first-world-cup: He's football's famous teenage star: under 20.
tour-de-france-stages: It lasts three weeks and they race almost every day.
paris-2024-events: Over 30 sports, each with several events (swimming and athletics have dozens): a few hundred.
ski-jump-record: A football pitch is about 100 m long; the best jumpers fly two or more pitches.
new-york-yellow-taxis: 8.8 million people and yellow cabs everywhere in Manhattan; one cab for every 500 to 1,000 people is about ten thousand.
magic-kingdom-visitors: A busy day brings tens of thousands through the gates; times 365 is ten to twenty million.
first-ipod-songs: An MP3 song is about 4 to 5 MB, and 5 GB is 5,000 MB: about a thousand.
mayflower-crossing: Lindbergh flew it in a day and a half; a slow sailing ship in autumn storms takes weeks, perhaps a couple of months.
pony-express-time: About 3,000 km on horseback with fresh horses, day and night; a horse relay might cover 300 km a day.
centennial-light: Famous record bulbs are 'over a century old', hand-made before cheap bulbs; count from around 1900.
four-k-pixels: 4K means about 4,000 pixels across; a 16:9 screen is a bit over half as tall: 4,000 x 2,000 is 8 million.
empire-state-lightning: New York gets thunderstorms on a few dozen days a year, and the tallest pointed thing around catches many of them.
all-gold-cube: Gold is about 19 times as heavy as water; 200,000 tonnes is about 10,000 cubic metres, a cube about 20 m across.
rubiks-cube-moves: Beginners' methods take about 100 moves and speedcubers about 50; a perfect solver needs fewer still.
film-frame-rate: Smooth motion needs a couple of dozen pictures a second; a flick book at 10 looks jerky.
cologne-cathedral-build: Medieval cathedrals took a century or more, and this one is famous for standing unfinished for ages: several hundred years.
mount-rushmore-carving: Four faces 18 m tall blasted out of granite by a few hundred workers in the 1930s: years, about a decade.
big-ben-bell-weight: A car weighs about 1.5 tonnes; a bell you can hear across London is much bigger than a car: around ten.
sydney-opera-house-build: A famously difficult building of the 1960s, late and over budget: well over the few years planned.
pentagon-corridors: Five sides, five rings of corridors, five floors: 25 rings of several hundred metres each, tens of kilometres.
st-peters-capacity: It's the biggest church in the world; a full football stadium holds 50,000 to 90,000.
earths-to-the-moon: Textbook pictures put the Moon close by, but light takes over a second to get there: tens of Earth widths, not a handful.
halleys-comet-return: It's famously seen once in a lifetime: a bit under a human lifespan.
apollo-moon-rock: Six landings, each bringing back a few boxes of rocks: tens of kilos each, a few hundred in all.
baumgartner-jump-height: Planes cruise at 10 to 12 km; he rose by balloon to the edge of space, several times higher.
james-webb-distance: Hubble orbits a few hundred km up; Webb went far past the Moon's 384,000 km: a million or so.
dinosaur-asteroid-width: Big enough to end the dinosaurs but small next to Earth's 12,700 km: kilometres, not hundreds.
wettest-place-rainfall: London gets about 600 mm a year and a monsoon city a few thousand; the wettest place must be several times that.
oldest-living-tree: Old redwoods and yews are a couple of thousand years old; the record holder is older than the Roman Empire.
antarctic-ice-thickness: Mountains there are buried with only their tips showing, and the highest Antarctic peaks are 4 to 5 km: a couple of km.
un-member-states: There are about 200 countries in the world, and nearly all of them are in.
equator-countries: Trace it on a map: Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil, then the middle of Africa, then Indonesia's islands.
busiest-airport-passengers: A big airport handles a plane a minute or more all day, about 150 people each: tens of millions to a hundred million.
us-golf-courses: Golf is big in America: thousands of towns, many with a course or two: over ten thousand.
pineapple-flowers: Count the diamond-shaped segments on a pineapple's skin: each is one of the fused fruits, a hundred or more.
colosseum-audience: A big modern stadium holds 50,000 to 90,000, and the Colosseum is the model for them.
right-eye-dominant-share: Most people are right-handed (about 90%), and eyes lean the same way but less: test it by pointing and closing each eye.
short-sighted-share: Count the glasses-wearers in your class (many for distance), then think of the whole world, where rates differ: a fifth or so.
blood-plasma-share: Blood looks red, but a blood bag left to stand separates into a red layer and a yellow one about as big.
brown-eyes-share: Think of the whole world, not just your street: Africa, Asia and the Americas are mostly brown-eyed.
blood-in-veins-share: Blood leaves the heart fast in thick arteries and comes back slowly in wider, stretchy veins, so it pools there: over half.
rice-maize-wheat-share: Picture plates worldwide: rice across Asia, bread and pasta in the West, maize in the Americas and Africa: most of it.
soy-for-livestock: You might think of tofu and soy milk, but soy is grown in vast fields in Brazil and the US for feed: most of it.
parmesan-milk-share: Italy makes hundreds of cheeses and drinks fresh milk, but Parmesan wheels are huge and need hundreds of litres each: a fifth or so.
farmland-share: Take away the oceans; deserts, ice, mountains and forests cover much of the land, and fields and pasture most of the rest: a third or more.
plastic-recycled-share: Recycling bins are recent and much plastic can't be reused; most of it is in landfill: well under a third.
france-nuclear-share: France is the famous nuclear country, with few coal or gas plants: more than half.
iceland-geothermal-share: Iceland is famous for hot springs, but also for big glacier rivers: its power could come from either.
cloud-cover-share: Look up on an average day, or at a satellite picture of Earth: more white than not.
amazon-river-flow-share: It's by far the biggest river; with hundreds of other big rivers worldwide, a fifth would already be huge.
mountainous-land-share: Picture the continents: the Himalayas, Andes, Rockies and Alps, but also vast plains and deserts: a quarter or so.
tropics-share: The tropics look like a thin band on a flat map, but a globe bulges at the middle: much more than a tenth.
lunar-maria-share: Look at the full Moon: the dark patches cover a third of the face or so; the far side has hardly any, so halve it.
moon-width-share: In photos of the Earth and Moon together, the Moon looks a quarter to a third as wide.
mars-mission-failures: Mars is famously hard to reach and land on, with many crashes in the news: around half.
octopus-arm-neurons: Eight long arms that taste, feel and move on their own against one small head: most of them.
perching-birds-share: Sparrows, robins, crows, finches and tits are everywhere; ducks, eagles and parrots are fewer kinds: over half.
free-ranging-dogs-share: Pet dogs fill parks in rich countries, but most of the world's dogs roam villages and streets: over half.
india-wild-tigers-share: Tigers also live in Russia, Indonesia, Nepal and Bangladesh, but India's reserves are the famous ones: over half.
world-literacy-share: Most children now go to school, but many adults in poorer countries never did: most, but not all.
english-wikipedia-share: English is the web's biggest language, but there are hundreds of Wikipedias, some of them huge: well under half.
welsh-speakers-share: Road signs are bilingual, but in Cardiff you mostly hear English: a minority, a fifth or so.
bank-account-share: Nearly everyone in rich countries has one, and mobile money has spread through Africa: most adults.
electric-car-sales-share: China sells huge numbers of electric cars, Europe many and the US fewer: about a quarter.
us-passport-share: Many Americans never travel abroad, but more do now and need one even for Canada and Mexico: around half.
under-15-share: Families are big in Africa and South Asia and small in Europe and East Asia: a quarter or so.
coastal-population-share: Think of the giant cities on the sea (Tokyo, Shanghai, Mumbai, New York, Lagos), but India and China have huge inland populations: under half.
great-wall-lost-share: It's centuries old, and long stretches have crumbled: a fair chunk, but most of it still stands.
women-first-at-olympics: The first modern Games had no women; they joined at one of the next few, in the early 1900s or just before.
first-london-marathon: Marathon running boomed after New York's race in the 1970s; London followed soon after.
uranus-discovered: It was the first planet found with a telescope, by an astronomer of Mozart's time: the late 1700s.
basketball-invented: It's a game older than the NBA (1940s) and played at college before then: the late 1800s.
first-f1-championship: Motor racing restarted after the Second World War, and the championship followed a few years later.
olympic-gold-silver-bronze: The first modern Games were in the 1890s, and the medal colours came at one of the next few Games.
insulin-first-used: Before antibiotics but after the First World War: diabetes was a death sentence until the 1920s.
aspirin-first-sold: A German company's chemistry at the end of the 1800s, before the First World War.
stethoscope-invented: Doctors in Napoleon's time put an ear to the chest; a tube to listen through came soon after.
suez-canal-opens: A Victorian engineering feat, decades before the Panama Canal (1914).
sagrada-familia-begun: Gaudí worked on it in the late 1800s and died in the 1920s with it far from finished.
tower-bridge-opens: Its Victorian Gothic towers and steam-powered lifting roadway date it to late Victorian London.
voyager-1-launch: It's famously been flying for nearly 50 years, launched in the 1970s alongside Star Wars.
earthrise-photo: Taken by astronauts orbiting the Moon, so in the Apollo years, just before the first landing.
first-spacewalk: A few years after the first person in space (1961), in the Soviet-American space race.
iss-first-crew: The station was built in the late 1990s and has been lived in for about a quarter of a century.
sony-walkman-launch: The cassette Walkman was the music player of the 1980s, before CDs took over.
toy-story-released: Woody and Buzz are a 90s childhood: the mid-1990s.
first-christmas-card: Victorian Britain invented many Christmas traditions, in the 1840s with A Christmas Carol.
first-bicycle: Before railways and pedals, in the early 1800s, as a way to get about without a horse.
tin-can-patent: Napoleon's armies needed food that kept, so preserving it was a Napoleonic-era invention.
dodo-last-seen: Dutch sailors found Mauritius around 1600, and the bird was gone within a lifetime.
dolly-the-sheep: Cloning was big news in the 1990s, before the human genome was read.
last-tasmanian-tiger: Black-and-white film exists of the last ones in a zoo: the early 20th century, between the wars.
mickey-mouse-debut: Early sound cartoons, Disney's beginnings: the late 1920s.
first-guinness-book: A post-war idea from a brewery boss to settle pub arguments: the 1950s.
first-bullet-train: Japan's post-war boom, ready for the Tokyo Olympics: the 1960s.
yellowstone-first-park: After the American Civil War (1860s) and the move west: the 1870s.
krakatoa-eruption: A famous Victorian disaster, reported worldwide by telegraph: the 1880s.
spotify-launch: Streaming arrived after the iPhone (2007) and before Instagram (2010).
apple-i-on-sale: Apple started in a garage in the 1970s, years before the Macintosh (1984).
name-country-as-many-people-as-germany: Germany has about 83 million: look for big countries a little smaller or larger, like Turkey, Iran or France.
name-country-as-many-people-as-japan: Japan has about 120 million: a step below the giants, like Mexico, the Philippines or Ethiopia.
name-country-as-many-people-as-tokyo: Tokyo is the world's biggest city, about 40 million: a mid-sized country, like Canada, Poland or Spain.
name-country-as-big-as-turkey: Turkey is a bit bigger than France: think of long or mid-sized countries, like Chile, Pakistan or Myanmar.
name-country-as-big-as-italy: Picture Italy's boot: about the size of Poland, Norway, Finland or the UK.
name-city-as-many-people-as-new-zealand: New Zealand has about 5 million: a big but not giant city, like Sydney, Madrid or Toronto.
name-city-as-many-people-as-texas: Texas has about 30 million: one of the world's megacities, like Mumbai, Manila or Jakarta.
name-us-state-as-many-people-as-netherla: The Netherlands has about 18 million: one of the big states, like New York, Florida or Pennsylvania.
name-us-state-as-many-people-as-hong-kon: Hong Kong has about 7.5 million: a mid-sized state, like Arizona, Washington or Massachusetts.
name-us-state-as-many-people-as-rome: Rome's area holds about 3.5 million: a smaller state, like Utah, Nevada or Oregon.
name-us-state-as-big-as-portugal: Portugal is small for a country: a mid-sized eastern state, like Maine, Indiana or Kentucky.
name-us-state-as-big-as-spain: Spain is one of Europe's biggest: only the largest states come close, like California or Texas.
name-country-as-dense-as-india: India is crowded: think of other packed countries, like Japan, the Philippines or Belgium.
name-country-as-dense-as-china: China feels crowded but has vast empty west: try ordinary European or Asian countries, like France or Thailand.
name-country-as-dense-as-united-states: The US is roomy: countries with big empty spaces, like Sweden, Estonia or Colombia.
